narr: A deep upper level trough was observed exiting the southern Rockies during the morning of February 15th, with southwesterly windflow ahead of the trough allowing for a fetch of deep moisture from the western Gulf of America. This moisture pooled along a warm front situated across from Kentucky into southwest Virginia, where precipitable water values increased from 0.6 to 0.7 inches at 7 am that morning, to around 1.1 to 1.2 inches by early afternoon, which would be around 2 standard deviations above normal for mid-February. While the warm front shifted northward to the west of the Appalachians, high pressure off the Atlantic coast that was wedged against the eastern face of the Appalachians delayed the northward progress of the warm front. As such, the front remained stationary, and provided the focus for training of bands of heavy rain that fell across southwest Virginia through much of the day on February 15th. The rain fell at rates of 0.3 to 0.5 per hour beginning at around 9 am EST in the morning, which persisted for a 9-10 hour period. Rainfall totals ranged from 2 to 3 inches across southwest Virginia during this period. Soils across the area were nearly saturated from 2 rounds of widespread precipitation that fell earlier in the month. Additionally, the rain was falling over ground that was partially frozen, and covered in snow and ice from a winter storm that impacted southwest and central Virginia a few days earlier, increasing the rapid runoff potential into the creeks and rivers. In this event, CREST Unit Streamflow did not show impressive returns, while MRMS underestimated some of the precipitation totals. It was those factors combined with the high runoff potential of the rainfall that resulted in a lack of realization how quickly river levels were rising, and just how intense the flooding was becoming, even as far east as Appomattox County. CREST Hydrophobic Unit Flow proved to be a more accurate tool in this situation given the frozen ground, with returns as high as 480 cfs/m^2 across Giles County, which is where some of the most intense flooding was observed. Because MRMS was underestimating rainfall amounts, both the FLASH ARI and QPE/FFG values were also significantly underestimated. In these situation, monitoring ground-truth precipitation totals from a network of private weather stations might have prompted Flash Flood Warnings to be issued sooner.
ev: Tom's creek was observed rising rapidly out of its banks at multiple locations. Water was observed flowing across Coal Bank Hollow Road near Highway 460, and flooded the nearby Montgomery County Waste Site, causing damage to one of the service buildings located there. Further downstream, water was also observed flowing across Tom's Creek Road several inches deep.

A vehicle with a single occupant was pushed off of Kimberling Road into deeper water as Kimberling Creek flooded at least 2 feet over the roadway. The occupant attempted to abandon the vehicle, but was swept away by the flooding and passed away. Nearby, Wesendonck Road was observed flooded and impassible at several locations due to multiple creeks overflowing their banks. This includes Nobusiness Creek.

Spring Branch was observed overflowing its banks at several locations, and was flowing several inches deep across multiple roads in the Shawsville community. No damage was reported to the roads, which were open to traffic after the flooding receded.

Plum Creek was observed overflowing its banks, and was flowing several inches deep across Plum Creek Road, as well as within several nearby properties. No damage was reported, with Plum Creek Road open to traffic after the flooding receded. Property damage is the estimated cost of cleanup of the nearby properties.

The North Fork Roanoke River was observed overflowing its banks at several locations, and began flowing up to 2 feet deep across fields and properties along Catawba Road and Lusters Gate Road. Clubhouse Road was also flooded and impassible until the water receded. No damage was reported to the roads, which were open to traffic after the flooding receded.

Den Hill Creek was observed overflowing its banks several inches deep across Den Hill Road at multiple locations, making the road impassible. No damage was reported to the road, which was open to traffic after the flooding receded, though large pieces of debris needed to be cleaned off the road. Property damage is the estimated cost of the cleanup of the road.
Horners Branch was observed flowing out of its banks up to 3 feet deep across Main Street in the City of Salem. Multiple cars were reported stalled in the floodwaters.
Several roads were reported flooded and impassible in the area surrounding Roanoke College.
The Bluestone River was observed overflowing its banks and flooded across portions of both Meredith Street and Tazewell Avenue.

Numerous roads were reported flooded and impassible throughout the Town of Richlands due to flash flooding. This includes Ravens Nest Branch Road and Laurel Road due to flash flooding of Laurel Branch. Burnette Street near the intersection with Cliff Street was also observed flooded and impassible as a tributary of the Clinch River rose out of its banks. Near Cedar Bluff, portions of Bane Bottom Road were flooded by flooding of Indian Creek, with water approaching homes along the road.
North Creek was observed overflowing its banks and inundating North Creek Road several inches deep. No damage was reported to the roadway, which was open to traffic after the flooding receded.

Archer Creek was observed overflowing its banks about 1 foot deep across Stage Road, making the road impassible. No damage was reported to the road, which was open to traffic after the flooding receded, though pictures indicate that the road was covered in debris. Property damage is the estimated cost of clearing the debris from the road to make it passible.

Little Opossum Creek was observed overflowing its banks and inundating Holcomb Path Road several inches deep. No damage was reported to the roadway, which was open to traffic after the flooding receded.

Multiple creeks in and around the town of Saltville and across the northern half of Smyth County were observed overflowing their banks across nearby roads, causing them to become impassible. Possum Hollow Road was reported flooded as Beaver Creek rose out of its banks. Glade Branch was observed overflowing its banks several inches deep across Citizens Road, causing the road to be impassible until the flooding receded. No damage was reported to the road, which was reopened to traffic after the flooding receded. Social Media video indicates that the Well Fields in the town of Saltville flooded out of their banks across Palmer Avenue nearly a foot deep in spots. The parking lot of Food Country and Subway was also flooded by the Well Fields.

Numerous creeks and streams throughout the county were observed flowing out of their banks and onto nearby roads or over bridges. Roads that were flooded and impassible include Annie Akers Road, Lowman's Ferry Road, Gill Lane, Highland Road, Parrott River Road, Old Route 100, Fairlawn Road, Cox Hollow Road, Pond Lick Hollow Road, Buena Vista Road, Hilton Village Loop, Little Creek Road and Cleburne Boulevard. A trained Skywarn Spotter reported that Brookmont Road was flooded as Tract Fork rose out of its banks. WDBJ7 reported that several private bridges over creeks throughout the county that provide access to homes were heavily damaged or destroyed during the flooding.
Spruce Run was observed overflowing its banks, and was flowing several inches deep across Spruce Run Road. No damage was reported to the road, which was open to traffic after the flooding receded.
Numerous creeks and streams were reported flooded out of their banks and across several roads throughout the county, making them impassible until the flood waters receded.
